title: Can Brussels Budget Like a Superpower?
gist: The European Commission's proposed 2028-2034 EU budget of nearly 2 trillion euros (vs 1.2 trillion in 2021) would be the largest ever, with 451 billion for a Competitiveness Fund; the author argues success hinges on member-state cohesion amid Russian threat, weak Germany and France, and Trump-era distrust of the US.

themes.theme: Scale and composition of the proposal

insights.claim: The Commission proposed a 2028-2034 EU budget of nearly 2 trillion euros, the largest multiyear budget in the bloc's history, versus 1.2 trillion euros agreed in 2021 in current prices.
insights.speaker: Luke McGee
insights.so_what: A near 65 percent nominal step-up signals a structural shift toward EU-level fiscal capacity; the final number will be negotiated down.
insights.locator: The European Commission, the EU's executive arm

insights.claim: 451 billion euros of the proposal go to a Competitiveness Fund: 175 billion for scientific research, 131 billion for defense and space, and 144 billion for digital, healthcare, agriculture and green initiatives.
insights.speaker: Luke McGee
insights.so_what: Defense and space plus research spending are the budget lines most relevant to European industrial and defense equities.

insights.claim: The proposal earmarks 200 billion euros for the EU's global interests, including 100 billion euros for Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Luke McGee
insights.so_what: Multi-year Ukraine funding visibility, if approved, reduces annual financing risk for Kyiv.

insights.claim: EU budget figures understate European power because member-state spending is far larger: combined defense spending of EU members that are also in NATO exceeded $450 billion in 2025.
insights.speaker: Luke McGee
insights.so_what: Compare EU-budget lines to national budgets when sizing defense procurement potential.
insights.locator: For context, the combined total defense spending

insights.claim: EU diplomats say the overall figure of 2 trillion euros is too high and want it to come down, but a growing group of realists and pragmatists is pushing for cohesion spending as the way to hold the bloc together.
insights.speaker: Luke McGee
insights.so_what: Expect a lower final headline number with cohesion funds protected; watch frugal-state positioning.
insights.locator: The cohesion stuff has to happen

insights.claim: Weakness of Germany (far-right gains) and France (looming presidential election) is pushing smaller realist states to club together, and a Euroskeptic French successor wanting a Brussels-centric budget legacy could even bring France into the frugal camp.
insights.speaker: Luke McGee
insights.so_what: A French political shift could change the frugal-versus-spender balance in budget talks.
insights.locator: With Germany and France looking as weak

insights.claim: Euroskeptic resistance, skepticism in the European Parliament toward Commission spending, and domestic politics in each member state make approval of such a huge budget contentious.
insights.speaker: Luke McGee
insights.so_what: Approval is not assured; delays or deep cuts are a base-case risk.
insights.locator: Approving such a huge sum is also contentious

insights.claim: The author argues Putin's threat to the bloc is existential and many European countries are radically unprepared for war with Moscow, so Europe's security depends on acting as a cohesive unit and eventually ending reliance on the US.
insights.speaker: Luke McGee
insights.so_what: Underpins a multi-year European defense spending trajectory.
insights.locator: In 2026, that leveling up is about more than economics

insights.claim: If the Commission gets the money, cohesion and politics it wants, Europe could stop choosing between Washington and Beijing and start making its own rules.
insights.speaker: Luke McGee
insights.so_what: Long-run upside scenario for EU geopolitical weight; contingent on politics.
